Let $(S,m)$ be a finite Coxeter matrix, $W$ its presented group with length $\ell$ and standard parabolic subgroup $W_J=\langle J\rangle$ for $J\subseteq S$ ([[def-hh-coxeter-matrix-word-group-and-length]]). Let $R$, $H$, and the standard basis $\{T_w:w\in W\}$ be those of [[def-hh-universal-coxeter-hecke-parameters-and-presentation]] and [[thm-hh-generic-coxeter-hecke-standard-basis]]. Use the inherited parameters $v_j$ on the restricted Coxeter system $W_J$; distinct odd-edge components of $J$ may therefore carry the same parameter when they lie in one odd-edge component of $S$.

**Parabolic Hecke subalgebra.** Define the candidate $R$-submodule
$$
H_J:=\bigoplus_{u\in W_J}R T_u\subseteq H.
$$
The justifying theorem [[thm-hh-parabolic-hecke-freeness-and-induced-bases]] proves it is a subalgebra, is generated by $T_j$ for $j\in J$, and is the embedded image of the restricted-system Hecke algebra over $R$. The same theorem proves the left and right freeness assertions needed by the induced-module construction below.

For a left $H_J$-module $M$, define its **parabolic induction** to be the balanced tensor product
$$
\operatorname{Ind}_{J}^{W}(M):=H\otimes_{H_J}M,
$$
formed from the right $H_J$-module $H$ and left $H_J$-module $M$ ([[def-tensor-product-of-modules-by-generators-and-relations]], [[thm-universal-property-of-module-tensor-products]]). Thus $(h k)\otimes m=h\otimes(km)$ for $h\in H$, $k\in H_J$, and $m\in M$. The left $H$-action is $a\cdot(h\otimes m)=(ah)\otimes m$; it respects balancing because $(ahk)\otimes m=(ah)\otimes(km)$, and its module laws follow from associativity and the unit of $H$.

For a left $H$-module $N$, define **parabolic restriction** $\operatorname{Res}_{J}^{W}(N)$ to be its underlying $R$-module with the $H_J$-action obtained from the inclusion $H_J\hookrightarrow H$ proved by the same justifier. These constructions use left modules throughout; the theorem below also records the opposite right-module decomposition of $H$ so the two coset conventions remain explicit.

Let $(S,m)$, $W$, $\ell$ be as in [[def-hh-coxeter-matrix-word-group-and-length]]; let $R$, $v_s$, $H$, $T_s$ be as in [[def-hh-universal-coxeter-hecke-parameters-and-presentation]]; let $T_w$ for $w\in W$ and the spanning statement be as in [[lem-hh-reduced-word-independence-and-length-multiplication]]; and let $E$, $P_s$, $Q_s$ and $P_w$ be as in [[lem-hh-commuting-left-right-hecke-length-operators]].

1. **The length-operator representation.** There is a unique unital $R$-algebra homomorphism $\rho:H\to\operatorname{End}_R(E)$ with $\rho(T_s)=P_s$ for all $s\in S$; it satisfies $\rho(T_w)=P_w$ and $\rho(T_w)(e_1)=e_w$ for all $w\in W$.
2. **Standard basis.** $\{T_w:w\in W\}$ is an $R$-basis of $H$: it spans by [[lem-hh-reduced-word-independence-and-length-multiplication]] and is $R$-linearly independent. Hence $H$ is free as an $R$-module and every element of $H$ has a unique expansion $\sum_wa_wT_w$ with $a_w\in R$ and all but finitely many $a_w$ zero.
3. **Faithfulness.** $\rho$ is injective.
4. **Base change.** For every commutative ring $R'$ and every ring homomorphism $\varphi:R\to R'$, the scalar extension $R'\otimes_RH$ is, as an $R'$-algebra, canonically isomorphic to the quotient of the free associative $R'$-algebra on $(T_s)_{s\in S}$ by the two-sided ideal generated by the images under $\varphi$ of the relations (Q) and (B) of [[def-hh-universal-coxeter-hecke-parameters-and-presentation]], and it is free as an $R'$-module with basis $(1\otimes T_w)_{w\in W}$. No flatness or freeness of $R'$ over $R$ is assumed, and no torsion-freeness or semisimplicity of $H$ or of its specialisations is claimed.

Let $(S,m)$, $W$, $\ell$ be as in [[def-hh-coxeter-matrix-word-group-and-length]], and let $R$, $v_s$, $H$ and the generators $T_s$ be as in [[def-hh-universal-coxeter-hecke-parameters-and-presentation]].

1. **Well-defined reduced products.** If $w=s_1\cdots s_k$ and $w=s'_1\cdots s'_k$ are reduced expressions of $w\in W$ (so $k=\ell(w)$), then
$$T_{s_1}\cdots T_{s_k}=T_{s'_1}\cdots T_{s'_k}\quad\text{in }H.$$
Hence $T_w:=T_{s_1}\cdots T_{s_k}$ is a well-defined element of $H$ depending only on $w$; in particular $T_1=1$ (the empty product).

2. **Length-multiplication rules.** For all $s\in S$ and $w\in W$,
$$T_sT_w=\begin{cases}T_{sw},&\ell(sw)=\ell(w)+1,\\[2pt] T_{sw}+(v_s-v_s^{-1})T_w,&\ell(sw)=\ell(w)-1,\end{cases}\qquad T_wT_s=\begin{cases}T_{ws},&\ell(ws)=\ell(w)+1,\\[2pt] T_{ws}+(v_s-v_s^{-1})T_w,&\ell(ws)=\ell(w)-1.\end{cases}$$
(Exactly one case occurs, by [[thm-hh-coxeter-exchange-deletion-and-faithfulness]], part 1.)

3. **Spanning.** Every product $T_{s_1}\cdots T_{s_k}$ of generators is a finite $R$-linear combination of the elements $T_w$, and consequently $\{T_w:w\in W\}$ spans $H$ as an $R$-module: every element of $H$ is a finite sum $\sum_wa_wT_w$ with $a_w\in R$.

4. **Scope.** No independence or freeness of $\{T_w\}$ is asserted here; that is [[thm-hh-generic-coxeter-hecke-standard-basis]].

Let $(S,m)$ be a finite Coxeter matrix with presented group $W$, length $\ell$ and geometric representation $\sigma:W\to\mathrm{GL}_K(E)$ as in [[def-hh-coxeter-matrix-word-group-and-length]], [[def-hh-geometric-coxeter-representation-and-roots]] and [[lem-hh-dihedral-root-recurrence-and-root-sign]], and let $J\subseteq S$.

1. **Support and reduction.** For every $w\in W$ the set $S(w)$ of letters occurring in a reduced expression of $w$ is independent of the reduced expression, and every word in $S$ representing $w$ can be transformed into a reduced expression by repeatedly deleting two letters (Tits reduction, using only letters already present). Consequently
$$W_J=\langle J\rangle=\{w\in W:S(w)\subseteq J\}.$$
2. **Intrinsic parabolic presentation.** Let $W_J^\ast$ be the group presented by the restricted Coxeter matrix $(J,m|_J)$ in the sense of [[def-hh-coxeter-matrix-word-group-and-length]]. The canonical homomorphism $W_J^\ast\to W_J$, $s\mapsto s$, is an isomorphism. Hence $(W_J,J)$ is a Coxeter system, its intrinsic length function $\ell_J$ agrees with the ambient length $\ell$ on $W_J$, and $W_J\cap S=J$.
3. **Minimal coset representatives.** Every right coset $W_J a:=\{ua:u\in W_J\}$ ($a\in W$, [[def-coset]]) has a unique element $d$ of minimal length; it is characterized by $\ell(sd)>\ell(d)$ for all $s\in J$, and it satisfies
$$\ell(ud)=\ell(u)+\ell(d)\qquad\text{for all }u\in W_J .$$
Equivalently, every $w\in W$ has a unique factorization $w=u\,d$ with $u\in W_J$ and $d$ the minimal representative of the right coset $W_J d$, and then $\ell(w)=\ell(u)+\ell(d)$. By inversion ($w\mapsto w^{-1}$ preserves lengths and interchanges the two coset families $\{W_Ja\}$ and $\{aW_J\}$), every left coset $aW_J:=\{au:u\in W_J\}$ has a unique minimal element $d$, characterized by $\ell(ds)>\ell(d)$ for all $s\in J$ and satisfying $\ell(du)=\ell(d)+\ell(u)$ for all $u\in W_J$.
4. **Type A.** Let $n\ge2$, $S=\{s_1,\dots,s_{n-1}\}$ and $m(s_i,s_j):=3$ if $|i-j|=1$, $m(s_i,s_j):=2$ if $|i-j|>1$ (a Coxeter matrix of type $A_{n-1}$). Then $s_i\mapsto(i\ i+1)$ extends to an isomorphism $W\to S_n$ (the letters $1,\dots,n$ carry the library's symmetric group by the order-preserving identification with $\{0,\dots,n-1\}$, under which $(i\ i+1)$ is the adjacent transposition $(i-1\ i)$), and for every $w\in W$,
$$\ell(w)=\operatorname{inv}\bigl(\varphi(w)\bigr),$$
the inversion number of the corresponding permutation ([[def-inversions-inversion-number-and-sign]]). In particular a word in the $s_i$ is reduced if and only if its length equals the inversion number of its value.

Let $G$ be a group and let $H\le G$ be a subgroup ([[def-group]],
[[def-subgroup]]). For $g\in G$, the **left coset** and **right coset** of $H$
represented by $g$ are

$$gH:=\{gh:h\in H\},\qquad Hg:=\{hg:h\in H\}.$$

The element $g$ is a **representative** of these cosets. The notation denotes
subsets of $G$; it does not assert that either subset is a subgroup.

the inversion number of the corresponding permutation ([[def-inversions-inversion-number-and-sign]]). In particular a word in the $s_i$ is reduced if and only if its length equals the inversion number of its value.

Let $(S,m)$ be a finite Coxeter matrix, $W$ the presented group and $\ell$ its length function ([[def-hh-coxeter-matrix-word-group-and-length]]). Write $s\sim t$ when there exist $s=s_0,s_1,\dots,s_k=t$ in $S$ with $m(s_i,s_{i+1})$ odd for every $i<k$; this is the connected-component relation of the graph on $S$ whose edges are the pairs with odd $m$, and it is an equivalence relation (1.1). Let $[s]$ denote the class of $s$ and let $c$ be the number of classes.

**Coefficient ring.** Put $R:=\mathbb Z[v_1^{\pm1},\dots,v_c^{\pm1}]=\Lambda_{\mathbb Z,c}$, the Laurent polynomial ring in $c$ variables ([[lem-hh-finite-polynomial-and-localization-constructions]], part 2): a commutative ring in which every $v_i$ is a unit. Identify the classes with $\{1,\dots,c\}$ and put $v_s:=v_{[s]}\in R^\times$ for $s\in S$.

**The generic Hecke algebra.** Let $F:=R\langle T_s:s\in S\rangle$ be the free associative $R$-algebra on $S$ and let $I\subseteq F$ be the two-sided ideal generated ([[lem-hh-free-associative-ring-and-relations-descent]], part 2) by the **quadratic relations**
$$(T_s-v_s)(T_s+v_s^{-1})\qquad(s\in S)$$
and the **braid relations**
$$T_sT_tT_s\cdots=T_tT_sT_t\cdots\qquad(s\ne t,\ m(s,t)<\infty),$$
both alternating products having $m(s,t)$ factors. Define $H:=H(W):=F/I$ and write $T_s$ for the image of the generator $T_s$. Then $H$ is a unital associative $R$-algebra ([[def-algebra-over-a-commutative-ring]]) with the following **universal property**: for every unital associative $R$-algebra $A$ and every family $(t_s)_{s\in S}$ in $A$ satisfying the same two families of relations, there is a unique unital $R$-algebra homomorphism $H\to A$ with $T_s\mapsto t_s$.

**Universal parameters.** For every commutative ring $A$ and units $u_1,\dots,u_c\in A^\times$ the assignment $v_i\mapsto u_i$ extends uniquely to a ring homomorphism $R\to A$ ([[lem-hh-finite-polynomial-and-localization-constructions]], part 2); via the universal property of $H$ this makes $R$ the universal coefficient ring for a unit-valued parameter that is constant on each class $[s]$.

**Generator conjugacy.** Two simple generators $s,t\in S$ are conjugate in $W$ if and only if $s\sim t$.

**Conventions and scope.** (i) $m(s,t)=\infty$ imposes no relation between $T_s$ and $T_t$; if $c=1$ we write $v$ for $v_1$. (ii) The quadratic relation is equivalent to $T_s^2-(v_s-v_s^{-1})T_s-1=0$, equivalently $(T_s+v_s^{-1})(T_s-v_s)=0$, and it depends on $v_s$ only through the difference $v_s-v_s^{-1}$ (1.6). (iii) No freeness, torsion-freeness, specialisation or basis property of $H$ is asserted here: the elements $T_w$ are introduced in [[lem-hh-reduced-word-independence-and-length-multiplication]], their independence is proved in [[thm-hh-generic-coxeter-hecke-standard-basis]], and the invertibility and bar properties are recorded in [[lem-hh-hecke-anti-involution-bar-and-normalization]]; consumers may not use those features before those items.

derivations.claim: Let $K_J:=\bigoplus_{u\in W_J}RT_u$. If $u\in W_J$ and $j\in J$, the left and right length-multiplication rules in [F3] express $T_jT_u$ and $T_uT_j$ as linear combinations of $T_{ju},T_u$ and $T_{uj},T_u$ respectively; since $ju,uj\in W_J$, both products lie in $K_J$. Each $T_u$ is a product of the generators indexed by $J$, so $K_J$ contains the subalgebra they generate; conversely it is closed under multiplication by every such generator and contains $1$, so every word in those generators lies in $K_J$. Hence $K_J$ is exactly that generated subalgebra.

For each $w\in W$, [F4] gives a unique factorization $w=ud$ with $u\in W_J$ and $d\in D_R(J)$ and $\ell(w)=\ell(u)+\ell(d)$. Thus $W_Jd$ is the right coset represented by $d$ under [F5]. Choose reduced expressions for $u$ and $d$; their concatenation has length $\ell(u)+\ell(d)=\ell(ud)$ and so is reduced, giving $T_w=T_uT_d$ by [F3]. Thus the elements of $H_JT_d$ span $H$. If a finite sum $\sum_d h_dT_d=0$ with $h_d\in H_J$ is given, expand each $h_d$ as a finite sum $\sum_{u\in W_J}r_{u,d}T_u$ using [F1]. The resulting sum is $\sum_{u,d}r_{u,d}T_{ud}=0$. Unique factorization makes the elements $ud$ distinct for distinct pairs $(u,d)$; linear independence of the standard basis [F2] forces every $r_{u,d}=0$. This proves the left-module direct sum and its basis.

For each $w\in W$, the left-coset part of [F4] gives a unique factorization $w=du$ with $d\in D_L(J)$, $u\in W_J$, and $\ell(w)=\ell(d)+\ell(u)$. By [F5], $dW_J$ is the left coset represented by $d$. Reduced expressions for $d$ followed by $u$ concatenate to a reduced expression of $du$, so $T_w=T_dT_u$ by [F3]. Hence the elements of $T_dH_J$ span $H$. If $\sum_dT_dh_d=0$, expand $h_d=\sum_{u\in W_J}r_{d,u}T_u$; unique left-coset factorization makes all $du$ distinct, and [F2] then forces every coefficient to vanish. This proves the right-module direct sum and its basis.

By [F4], $(W_J,J)$ is a Coxeter system. Any odd-edge path in $J$ is also an odd-edge path in $S$, so the inherited parameters agree along every odd component of $J$ and give a ring map from the restricted system's universal parameter ring to $R$. Thus [F6] supplies a homomorphism from the restricted Hecke presentation to $H$ sending each $T_j$ to $T_j$. Apply the standard-basis theorem [F2] to the restricted system and this parameter map: its standard elements $T_u$ form an $R$-basis. Their images are the correspondingly named elements of the ambient $H$-basis, so the map is injective; its image is $K_J$ by step 1.1 and because every $u\in W_J$ has a word in $J$. Thus the candidate in [F1] is an embedded subalgebra, proving part 1.

By step 1.3, every $h\in H$ has a unique finite expansion $h=\sum_{d\in D_L(J)}T_dk_d$ with $k_d\in H_J$. Define $\Phi:\bigoplus_{d\in D_L(J)}M\to H\otimes_{H_J}M$ by $(m_d)_d\mapsto\sum_dT_d\otimes m_d$, and define $\Psi(h\otimes m):=(k_dm)_d$. The latter respects the balancing relation: the coefficients of $hk$ are $k_dk$, so $\Psi(hk\otimes m)=(k_d(km))_d=\Psi(h\otimes km)$. Uniqueness of the expansion shows $\Psi\Phi$ and $\Phi\Psi$ are identities. Thus $H\otimes_{H_J}M\cong\bigoplus_{d\in D_L(J)}M$; if $B$ is an $R$-basis of $M$, the displayed tensors form an $R$-basis.

For an $H_J$-linear map $g:M\to\operatorname{Res}_J^W N$, the formula $\widetilde g(h\otimes m)=h g(m)$ is balanced because $hk g(m)=h g(km)$, and it is $H$-linear. Conversely, if $F:H\otimes_{H_J}M\to N$ is $H$-linear, $m\mapsto F(1\otimes m)$ is $H_J$-linear since $1\otimes km=k\otimes m$. The two constructions are inverse: evaluation at $1\otimes m$ recovers $g(m)$, and $H$-linearity gives $F(h\otimes m)=hF(1\otimes m)$. This proves the adjunction.

The coset decompositions, their independence arguments, and the adjunction used no finiteness of $W$ and no choice of coset representatives: [F4] supplies each unique minimal representative. If $W$ is finite, each coset has $|W_J|$ elements, the cosets partition $W$, and the number of representatives is $|W|/|W_J|=[W:W_J]$. All coefficient arguments use standard bases and remain valid after any commutative base change of $R$ because the standard basis in [F2] does.

Let $(S,m)$ be a finite Coxeter matrix, $W$ the presented group and $\ell$ its length function ([[def-hh-coxeter-matrix-word-group-and-length]]). Write $s\sim t$ when there exist $s=s_0,s_1,\dots,s_k=t$ in $S$ with $m(s_i,s_{i+1})$ odd for every $i<k$; this is the connected-component relation of the graph on $S$ whose edges are the pairs with odd $m$, and it is an equivalence relation (1.1). Let $[s]$ denote the class of $s$ and let $c$ be the number of classes.

**Coefficient ring.** Put $R:=\mathbb Z[v_1^{\pm1},\dots,v_c^{\pm1}]=\Lambda_{\mathbb Z,c}$, the Laurent polynomial ring in $c$ variables ([[lem-hh-finite-polynomial-and-localization-constructions]], part 2): a commutative ring in which every $v_i$ is a unit. Identify the classes with $\{1,\dots,c\}$ and put $v_s:=v_{[s]}\in R^\times$ for $s\in S$.

**The generic Hecke algebra.** Let $F:=R\langle T_s:s\in S\rangle$ be the free associative $R$-algebra on $S$ and let $I\subseteq F$ be the two-sided ideal generated ([[lem-hh-free-associative-ring-and-relations-descent]], part 2) by the **quadratic relations**
$$(T_s-v_s)(T_s+v_s^{-1})\qquad(s\in S)$$
and the **braid relations**
$$T_sT_tT_s\cdots=T_tT_sT_t\cdots\qquad(s\ne t,\ m(s,t)<\infty),$$
both alternating products having $m(s,t)$ factors. Define $H:=H(W):=F/I$ and write $T_s$ for the image of the generator $T_s$. Then $H$ is a unital associative $R$-algebra ([[def-algebra-over-a-commutative-ring]]) with the following **universal property**: for every unital associative $R$-algebra $A$ and every family $(t_s)_{s\in S}$ in $A$ satisfying the same two families of relations, there is a unique unital $R$-algebra homomorphism $H\to A$ with $T_s\mapsto t_s$.

**Universal parameters.** For every commutative ring $A$ and units $u_1,\dots,u_c\in A^\times$ the assignment $v_i\mapsto u_i$ extends uniquely to a ring homomorphism $R\to A$ ([[lem-hh-finite-polynomial-and-localization-constructions]], part 2); via the universal property of $H$ this makes $R$ the universal coefficient ring for a unit-valued parameter that is constant on each class $[s]$.

**Generator conjugacy.** Two simple generators $s,t\in S$ are conjugate in $W$ if and only if $s\sim t$.

**Conventions and scope.** (i) $m(s,t)=\infty$ imposes no relation between $T_s$ and $T_t$; if $c=1$ we write $v$ for $v_1$. (ii) The quadratic relation is equivalent to $T_s^2-(v_s-v_s^{-1})T_s-1=0$, equivalently $(T_s+v_s^{-1})(T_s-v_s)=0$, and it depends on $v_s$ only through the difference $v_s-v_s^{-1}$ (1.6). (iii) No freeness, torsion-freeness, specialisation or basis property of $H$ is asserted here: the elements $T_w$ are introduced in [[lem-hh-reduced-word-independence-and-length-multiplication]], their independence is proved in [[thm-hh-generic-coxeter-hecke-standard-basis]], and the invertibility and bar properties are recorded in [[lem-hh-hecke-anti-involution-bar-and-normalization]]; consumers may not use those features before those items.

2. **Standard basis.** $\{T_w:w\in W\}$ is an $R$-basis of $H$: it spans by [[lem-hh-reduced-word-independence-and-length-multiplication]] and is $R$-linearly independent. Hence $H$ is free as an $R$-module and every element of $H$ has a unique expansion $\sum_wa_wT_w$ with $a_w\in R$ and all but finitely many $a_w$ zero.

No flatness or freeness of $R'$ over $R$ is assumed, and no torsion-freeness or semisimplicity of $H$ or of its specialisations is claimed.

Let $(S,m)$, $W$, $R$, $H$, the standard basis $\{T_w:w\in W\}$, and the trace $\tau$ be as in [[def-hh-universal-coxeter-hecke-parameters-and-presentation]], [[thm-hh-generic-coxeter-hecke-standard-basis]], and [[def-hh-canonical-hecke-trace-and-symmetrizing-form]]. Assume $W$ is finite. On the finite free $R$-module $E=\bigoplus_{w\in W}Re_w$, define the coordinate pairing by $\langle e_x,e_y\rangle=\delta_{x,y}$ and extend $R$-bilinearly. For an endomorphism $A$ with $A(e_x)=\sum_y a_{y,x}e_y$, define its coordinate transpose by $A^t(e_y)=\sum_xa_{y,x}e_x$, so $\langle Au,v\rangle=\langle u,A^tv\rangle$. Let $P_s$ be the left length operator of [[lem-hh-commuting-left-right-hecke-length-operators]].

For all $x,y\in W$,
$$
\tau(T_xT_y)=\delta_{x^{-1},y}.
$$
Consequently $\tau(ab)=\tau(ba)$ for all $a,b\in H$, and the map $H\to\operatorname{Hom}_R(H,R)$, $a\mapsto[b\mapsto\tau(ab)]$, is an isomorphism. The basis dual to $\{T_w:w\in W\}$ for this pairing is $\{T_{w^{-1}}:w\in W\}$; it is the standard basis indexed by inverses, not the algebra-inverse family $\{T_w^{-1}\}$.

For every unital homomorphism of commutative rings $\phi:R\to R'$, the induced canonical trace on $R'\otimes_RH$ has the same basis-pair formula and is again symmetric and perfect. No semisimplicity, field, or nondegeneracy hypothesis is required.
A left $R$-module is **semisimple** when it is an internal direct sum of simple submodules, allowing the empty direct sum. Hence the zero module is semisimple.

A left $R$-module $M$ is **simple** if $M\ne0$ and its only submodules are
$0$ and $M$. Equivalently, $M\ne0$ and $M$ has no proper nonzero submodule.

derivations.claim: Since $i^{-1}=-i$, the specialization of the quadratic relation in [F1] is $(T-i)^2=0$. The specialized basis is $\{1,T\}$, so $\epsilon:=T-i$ is nonzero and $A\cong\mathbb C[\epsilon]/(\epsilon^2)$. The canonical trace has $\tau(1)=1$, $\tau(T)=0$, and $T^2=1+2iT$; therefore its Gram matrix in $(1,T)$ is $\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$. The algebra is commutative, so the trace is symmetric, and this matrix is invertible, so its trace pairing is perfect (also as guaranteed by [F2]).

As a left $A$-module, $A\epsilon=\mathbb C\epsilon$ is simple: $\epsilon$ acts as zero on this one-dimensional complex vector space, and scalar elements of $\mathbb C$ act by scalar multiplication, so its only $A$-submodules are $0$ and $\mathbb C\epsilon$ by [F4]. If $x=a+b\epsilon$ with $a\ne0$, then $x$ is a unit, with inverse $a^{-1}-a^{-2}b\epsilon$; hence $Ax=A$, which is not simple because it contains the proper nonzero submodule $\mathbb C\epsilon$. Thus a simple submodule cannot contain an element with nonzero constant coefficient. Every nonzero element with zero constant coefficient generates $\mathbb C\epsilon$, so every simple submodule of $A$ is exactly $\mathbb C\epsilon$.

The sum of all simple submodules of $A$ is consequently $\mathbb C\epsilon$, which is proper because $1\notin\mathbb C\epsilon$. By [F3], the regular module is not a direct sum of simple submodules, so it is not semisimple. Step 1.1 gives a perfect symmetric trace on this finite-dimensional algebra, while this step proves its regular module is not semisimple. This refutes the claim. No choice principle is used.
